title: RAG architecture: retrieve, then generate
objective: Explain why a language model needs retrieval, trace a query through a RAG pipeline, and choose a chunking strategy.

segments.title: Why a model needs retrieval
segments.narration_text: A language model only knows what it saw during training. Its knowledge is frozen, and it has never read your documents. Retrieval augmented generation fixes that. Before the model answers, we fetch the most relevant passages from your own data and place them in the prompt. Retrieve first, then generate.

segments.title: Trace a query through the pipeline
segments.narration_text: Follow one question through the system. The query is embedded into a vector. We search the vector database for the nearest chunks and keep the top k. Those chunks are inserted into the prompt as context, and the model writes an answer grounded in them. Every stage is something you will build this week.

segments.title: Chunking and grounding
segments.narration_text: Documents are split into chunks before they are embedded. Chunks that are too large blur the meaning; chunks that are too small lose context. A common starting point is around five hundred tokens with some overlap. Finally, ask the model to cite which chunk it used, so every answer can be checked.

checkpoint.prompt: Why ask the model to cite chunks?
checkpoint.answer: So every answer can be verified against its source.

quiz.prompt: What does retrieval add that the base model lacks?
quiz.explanation: The model's training data is frozen; retrieval brings in your own, current information.

quiz.prompt: Which stage decides what context the model sees?
quiz.explanation: The search and top-k step chooses which chunks enter the prompt.
